report:
**Conclusion:** For typical knee osteoarthritis, arthroscopy (lavage/debridement) does **not** provide meaningful benefit over placebo/sham or optimized non-surgical care, and major guidelines recommend against it. It should not be used simply to “clean out” an arthritic knee; a narrow exception is true mechanical locking from a loose body or comparable mechanical lesion, not pain alone.

Evidence: the landmark sham-controlled trial found arthroscopic debridement/lavage was no better than placebo for pain/function (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2818323/). A later randomized trial found arthroscopy added no benefit to optimized physical and medical therapy (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18784099/). The BMJ RapidRecs panel made a **strong recommendation against arthroscopy in nearly all patients with degenerative knee disease**, with or without imaging osteoarthritis or mechanical symptoms (https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982). AAOS likewise states arthroscopy with lavage and/or debridement is **not recommended** for a primary diagnosis of knee OA (https://www.aaos.org/globalassets/quality-and-practice-resources/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/oak3cpg.pdf).

Bottom line: prioritize exercise/physical therapy, weight management, analgesia, and consider injections or joint replacement when appropriate; reserve arthroscopy for selected mechanical indications after specialist evaluation.
